q: Explain retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and its main components.
a: RAG improves answers by fetching relevant information at request time and giving it to the model as context, instead of relying only on what it memorised. The pipeline has two sides. Offline ingestion loads documents, cleans and splits them into chunks, creates embeddings and stores them with metadata in a vector index or search engine. Online, the user's question is turned into a query, often rewritten, the retriever finds the most relevant chunks, optionally a reranker reorders them, and the prompt is built from the instructions, the retrieved context and the question. The model answers using that context, ideally with citations, and the application validates the output. RAG gives fresher knowledge, access to private data, source attribution, lower hallucination and no retraining when documents change. The trade-offs are more moving parts, retrieval quality as the dominant factor, added latency and the need to secure and update the index.
f: When is RAG better than fine-tuning?
What are the two failure points?
p: Ingest, chunk, embed and index offline; at query time retrieve, rerank, build the prompt and generate with citations. RAG adds fresh private knowledge without retraining, but retrieval quality dominates.
tip: Say retrieval quality is the thing that decides RAG quality.

q: How do you choose chunking strategy and chunk size for RAG?
a: Chunking determines what the retriever can find and what the model sees, so I treat it as a tuning parameter. Chunks that are too small lose context and produce fragments; chunks that are too large dilute the embedding, waste prompt tokens and bring in irrelevant text. A practical start is a few hundred tokens with a modest overlap, then I adjust by evaluation. I prefer structure-aware splitting that follows headings, paragraphs, code blocks and table boundaries, rather than blindly cutting at a character count, and I keep metadata such as title, section, source and date with every chunk. Advanced options include parent-child chunking, where small chunks are retrieved but the larger parent is sent to the model, and adding a short context summary to each chunk. I decide using a retrieval evaluation set, measuring recall and answer quality across different settings, not intuition.
f: What is parent-child retrieval?
Why keep overlap between chunks?
p: Start with a few hundred tokens and small overlap, split along document structure, keep metadata, consider parent-child retrieval, and tune with a retrieval evaluation set rather than intuition.
tip: Say you tune chunking against measured recall.

q: What is hybrid search and why combine keyword and vector retrieval?
a: Vector search finds semantically similar text, even with different wording, but it can miss exact terms such as product codes, error messages, names and rare acronyms. Keyword search, typically BM25, is excellent at exact matches but fails when the query uses different words than the document. Hybrid search runs both and merges their results, commonly with reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted score, so you get semantic recall and lexical precision. It is especially valuable for technical and enterprise content full of identifiers. Many systems, such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and several vector databases, offer it natively. After merging, a reranker can further improve the ordering. I validate that hybrid actually helps on my own queries by comparing recall against vector-only retrieval, and I tune the fusion weights, because the best mix depends on the content and query types.
f: What is reciprocal rank fusion?
Which queries do keyword indexes handle better?
p: Vector search handles meaning, BM25 handles exact identifiers; hybrid merges both with rank fusion for better recall and precision. Confirm gains with a retrieval evaluation set.
tip: Mention error codes and product names as the case for keywords.

q: What does a reranker do and when is it worth the added latency?
a: The first-stage retriever, usually embedding similarity, is fast but approximate: it scores the query and each chunk separately. A reranker is a cross-encoder model that reads the query and a candidate chunk together and produces a more accurate relevance score. The usual pattern is to retrieve a broad set, for example fifty candidates, rerank them, and send only the top handful to the language model. This raises precision, reduces noise and saves prompt tokens, which often improves answer quality more than switching the generator. The costs are extra latency, typically tens to a few hundred milliseconds depending on the model and number of candidates, and extra compute to host. I use a reranker when answers suffer from irrelevant context, when the corpus is large and noisy, or when the top few results matter most, and I confirm the benefit with an offline evaluation and a latency budget.
f: How many candidates would you rerank?
Cross-encoder versus bi-encoder?
p: A cross-encoder reranker scores query and chunk together, so retrieving many and reranking to a few raises precision and cuts prompt tokens, at some latency. Use it when context noise hurts answers.
cmds: scores = reranker.predict([(query, c.text) for c in candidates])
tip: Say retrieve wide, rerank narrow, then check the latency budget.

q: How do you choose a vector database or index for RAG?
a: I compare options against requirements rather than pick by fashion. Scale: a few million vectors can live happily in pgvector inside PostgreSQL, while hundreds of millions to billions point to a specialised engine or a distributed one. Query features: filtering by metadata, hybrid search, multi-tenancy, and updates and deletes with good performance. Operations: managed service versus self-hosting, backups, high availability, security controls, and integration with existing platforms, which is why many teams start with PostgreSQL or OpenSearch they already run. Index types matter: HNSW offers high recall and speed but uses memory, IVF and product quantisation trade accuracy for size. Cost and latency targets complete the picture. I benchmark candidates on my own data and filters measuring recall at a given latency, because published benchmarks may not match my workload, and I design so the index can be rebuilt from source documents.
f: HNSW versus IVF?
Why rebuildability matters?
p: Choose by scale, filtering and hybrid features, operations and security, index type and cost; benchmark recall versus latency on your data. pgvector is often enough to start, and the index must be rebuildable.
cmds: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
tip: Say start with what you already run, and benchmark on your data.

q: How do metadata filters and access control work in RAG, and why are they critical?
a: Every chunk should be stored with metadata: source document, owner or team, access control list, tenant, classification, language, date and version. At query time the retrieval step must apply filters derived from the authenticated user, so the search only returns chunks the user is allowed to see. This is essential, because a RAG system that ignores permissions can leak confidential documents through the model's answer, even if the original system would have denied access. I enforce this in the retrieval layer, not in the prompt, since a prompt instruction cannot reliably stop a model from revealing text it was given. For multi-tenant systems, I use per-tenant indexes or mandatory tenant filters tested for leaks. Permissions also change over time, so I sync access control updates and deletions promptly, and I audit which sources were used for each answer.
f: Why not enforce access in the prompt?
How do you keep ACLs in sync?
p: Store ACLs and tenant metadata with every chunk and filter at retrieval time using the user's identity. Never rely on the prompt for access control, sync permission changes and audit sources used.
cmds: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 5;
tip: Enforce permissions in retrieval; a prompt is not an access control.

q: How do you keep a RAG index fresh and handle updates and deletions?
a: I design ingestion as a pipeline with change detection. Sources emit events or are crawled on a schedule, and each document has a stable ID and a content hash, so I only re-process changed documents. Updating a document means deleting its old chunks by document ID and inserting the new ones, preferably in an atomic step or with versioning so queries never see a half-updated state. Deletions must propagate, which matters for compliance and for removing outdated or retracted content. I track freshness metadata, so the retriever can prefer recent versions and the answer can show the date. For embedding model changes or chunking changes, I build a new index alongside the old one, validate it on the evaluation set, then switch over, which gives a safe rollback. Monitoring ingestion lag, failures and index size keeps the system trustworthy.
f: How do you re-embed everything safely?
What do you monitor in ingestion?
p: Ingestion with stable IDs and content hashes, delete-and-reinsert per document, propagated deletions, freshness metadata, and blue-green rebuilds for embedding or chunking changes. Monitor lag and failures.
cmds: sha256sum docs/*.md > manifest.new && diff manifest.old manifest.new
tip: Blue-green indexes make embedding upgrades safe.

q: How do you evaluate a RAG system, separating retrieval quality from generation quality?
a: I measure the two stages independently, because the fixes are different. For retrieval, I build a set of questions with known relevant documents or passages and compute recall at k, mean reciprocal rank and precision, which tells me whether the right context is found. For generation, given the retrieved context, I assess faithfulness, meaning whether the answer is supported by the context, answer relevance to the question, completeness, and citation correctness. Tools like RAGAS, TruLens and custom rubrics, with an LLM as a judge calibrated against human labels, automate this. I also test refusal behaviour when the answer is not in the corpus, and robustness to paraphrased or adversarial questions. End-to-end, I track user feedback and escalation rates in production. When quality drops, the split tells me whether to fix chunking, embeddings and search, or the prompt and model.
f: What is faithfulness?
How do you build the question set?
p: Evaluate retrieval with recall at k and MRR against labelled passages, and generation with faithfulness, relevance, completeness and citation accuracy, plus refusal tests. The split tells you what to fix.
cmds: ragas evaluate --dataset qa.jsonl --metrics context_recall faithfulness answer_relevancy
tip: Separate retrieval from generation so you know which to fix.

q: Your RAG chatbot gives wrong answers even though the right document is in the index. How do you debug?
a: I trace one failing question through every stage. First, was the right chunk retrieved? I log the retrieved chunks and scores. If it is missing, the cause is in chunking, embeddings, query phrasing or filters, and I can try query rewriting, hybrid search or a different chunk size. If it was retrieved but ranked low, a reranker or a better top-k helps. If it was in the prompt but the model ignored it, the context may be too long and noisy, the key fact may be buried in the middle, or the instructions may not insist on using the context; I shorten the context and strengthen the instruction. If the chunk was cut so the answer is split across chunks, I increase overlap or use parent retrieval. I also check stale versions and access filters. Then I add this failing question to the evaluation set to prevent regression.
f: How do you log retrieval for debugging?
What is query rewriting?
p: Trace the failure stage by stage: was the chunk retrieved, ranked, included in the prompt and used? Fix chunking, hybrid search, reranking, context length or instructions accordingly, and add the case to the evaluation set.
cmds: python trace_query.py --q 'How do I rotate keys?' --show-chunks
tip: Walk the pipeline stage by stage and add the case to the evaluation set.

q: What is query rewriting and when does it help retrieval?
a: User questions are often short, ambiguous, conversational or full of pronouns, which makes them poor search queries. Query rewriting uses a model to transform the input into one or more better queries before retrieval. Examples include resolving references using conversation history, so that 'what about the second one' becomes a standalone question, expanding abbreviations and synonyms, splitting a compound question into sub-questions, or generating several paraphrases and merging the results. Another technique, hypothetical document embeddings, asks the model to write a plausible answer and uses that as the search vector. These steps improve recall, especially in multi-turn chat and for complex questions, at the cost of an extra model call, added latency, and the risk of drifting from the original intent. I add rewriting when evaluation shows recall problems, use a small fast model, and keep the original query as one of the searches.
f: What is HyDE?
How do you control the added latency?
p: A model rewrites or decomposes the query into standalone, expanded or multiple queries before retrieval, improving recall in chat and complex questions at the cost of latency and possible drift. Keep the original query too.
cmds: rewritten = llm('Rewrite as a standalone search query: ' + history + question)
tip: Keep the original query alongside the rewritten ones.

q: How do you handle PDFs, tables, images and other messy documents in ingestion?
a: Document quality sets the ceiling for RAG. For PDFs I first check whether they contain real text or scans; scans need OCR. Layout-aware parsers extract reading order, headings, columns, headers and footers, and I remove repeated boilerplate that pollutes chunks. Tables are tricky: flattening them to plain text loses structure, so I convert them to markdown or structured rows, keep the caption and headers with each row group, or index a generated description. Images and diagrams can be captioned by a vision model, with the caption indexed and the image reference kept. Code and configuration files are split by function or block. I preserve metadata such as page numbers for citation. I sample the parsed output and read it, because silent parsing errors are common, and I record parser versions so re-ingestion is reproducible. Good extraction usually helps more than a fancier model.
f: How do you test parsing quality?
What do you do with scanned documents?
p: Use layout-aware parsing and OCR for scans, strip boilerplate, convert tables to structured text with headers, caption images, split code by block, keep page metadata, and read samples of the parsed output.
tip: Say you read samples of the parsed output; silent failures are common.

q: What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning, and when do you combine them?
a: RAG supplies knowledge at request time. It is the right tool when the information changes, is private, large, or must be cited, and when you need to control access. Fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour: its style, format, domain vocabulary and task skill, and it is better for consistent tone, specialised output formats, or teaching a narrow skill. Fine-tuning is poor at injecting facts reliably and makes updates slow, since new knowledge needs retraining, while RAG updates by editing documents. They combine well: fine-tune for how the model should behave, for example how to read the retrieved context, cite and refuse, and use RAG for what it should know. I normally start with prompting, then add RAG, and only fine-tune when evaluation shows a behaviour gap that prompts cannot close, because fine-tuning adds data, training and versioning overhead.
f: Why is fine-tuning poor for facts?
What data would you need to fine-tune?
p: RAG gives fresh, private, citable knowledge; fine-tuning changes behaviour and format. Combine them: fine-tune for how, retrieve for what. Start with prompts, add RAG, and fine-tune only for proven behaviour gaps.
tip: Summarise: fine-tune for how, retrieve for what.

q: How do you add citations and grounding checks to RAG answers?
a: I make the model show its evidence and then verify it in code. The prompt supplies each chunk with an ID and instructs the model to answer only from the provided sources and to mark each claim with the ID of the supporting chunk, or to say that the answer is not in the sources. The application then post-processes: it checks that every cited ID actually exists in the retrieved set, renders those IDs as links to the original documents with page or section, and optionally verifies support. Verification can use a natural language inference model or a second LLM call that checks each statement against its cited text, flagging unsupported claims. If a claim is unsupported, I remove it, regenerate, or show a lower confidence message. Citations build user trust, speed fact checking and give me data to evaluate faithfulness, but they do not prove correctness, so critical use still needs review.
f: Why do cited IDs need to be checked?
What is an NLI check?
p: Give chunks IDs, require claim-level citations or an I-don't-know, then verify in code that IDs exist, link them to sources, and optionally check support with an NLI model or a second call. Citations aid trust but are not proof.
cmds: assert all(c in retrieved_ids for c in extract_citations(answer))
tip: Check cited IDs exist; models can invent them.

q: How do you reduce latency in a RAG pipeline?
a: I start by measuring each stage: query rewriting, embedding, vector search, reranking, prompt build, time to first token and generation. Then I optimise the largest. Run independent steps in parallel, such as keyword and vector search. Cache query embeddings and frequent answers. Use a smaller, faster embedding model or a local one to avoid network hops, tune the index, for example the HNSW ef_search parameter and the number of candidates, and keep the index in memory. Limit the reranker to a modest candidate set, or use a lighter reranker. Send fewer, better chunks to the model, which cuts prefill time. Stream the answer so users see tokens early, and use prompt caching for the static instructions. Place the services close together to reduce network latency. Finally, set a latency budget per stage and track p95 and p99, not only the average.
f: Which stage usually dominates?
How does streaming change perceived latency?
p: Measure each stage, parallelise independent steps, cache embeddings and answers, tune the index and candidate counts, shrink the context, stream output and use prompt caching, with budgets tracked at p95 and p99.
tip: Say you track p95 and p99 per stage.

q: What is GraphRAG and when would a knowledge graph help?
a: Plain RAG retrieves isolated chunks, which struggles with questions that need connections across many documents, such as which services depend on a failing component, or what are the main themes in this corpus. GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph, extracting entities and relationships from the text, often with an LLM, and then answers using graph traversal, community summaries or a combination with vector search. It helps with multi-hop reasoning, global summarisation questions, and domains where relationships are central, for example infrastructure dependencies, compliance, supply chains and incident history. The costs are significant: extraction is expensive and can be noisy, graphs need maintenance as data changes, and the pipeline is more complex. I would try it when evaluation shows multi-hop or global questions failing with standard retrieval, and when an existing graph, such as a CMDB or service catalogue, can be reused instead of generated from scratch.
f: What kinds of questions fail in plain RAG?
How do you keep a graph current?
p: GraphRAG extracts entities and relations into a graph to answer multi-hop and global questions that chunk retrieval misses. It is costly and complex, so try it when evaluation shows such failures, ideally reusing an existing graph like a CMDB.
tip: Reuse an existing graph such as a service catalogue if possible.

q: How do you secure a RAG system against data leakage and poisoned documents?
a: There are two risks. Leakage comes from missing or weak access control, from logging sensitive prompts and retrieved text, and from sending data to third-party models without agreements. I enforce permissions at retrieval, mask sensitive data during ingestion where required, encrypt the index and logs, and set retention limits. Poisoning means an attacker places content in a source the system ingests, such as a wiki page, ticket or email, containing false facts or hidden instructions that the model will follow when retrieved, which is indirect prompt injection. Defences include controlling who can write to ingested sources, reviewing and scanning documents on ingestion, tracking provenance and trust levels by source, separating retrieved text from instructions in the prompt, limiting what actions the model can take after reading it, and monitoring outputs for anomalies. I also keep audit logs of which documents were used, so that I can trace and remove bad content quickly.
f: What is provenance tracking?
How do you remove a poisoned document quickly?
p: Prevent leakage with retrieval-time access control, masking, encryption and retention. Prevent poisoning by controlling writers, scanning on ingestion, tracking provenance, separating data from instructions, limiting actions and auditing which documents were used.
tip: Name indirect prompt injection via ingested content.

q: What is an AI agent and how does it differ from a simple LLM call or a workflow?
a: A simple LLM call takes input and returns text. A workflow chains model calls and tools along a path that the developer defines in code, so the control flow is fixed and predictable. An agent lets the model decide the control flow: in a loop, it observes the state, chooses an action, usually a tool call, sees the result, and repeats until it decides the goal is met or a limit is reached. This flexibility lets agents handle open-ended tasks, such as investigating an incident across several systems, but it makes behaviour less predictable, harder to test, and more costly and slower, and it increases risk because the model chooses actions. My rule is to use the simplest design that works: a single call if possible, a workflow if the steps are known, and an agent only when the path genuinely cannot be predefined, with strong limits and monitoring.
f: When is a fixed workflow better than an agent?
What limits would you put on an agent loop?
p: A call returns text, a workflow follows developer-defined steps, and an agent lets the model choose actions in a loop. Agents are flexible but less predictable, so use the simplest design that works and add limits.
cmds: while not done and steps < MAX_STEPS: action = llm(state); state = run(action)
tip: Say simplest design that works: call, then workflow, then agent.

q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and why does it matter for platform teams?
a: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that defines how AI applications connect to external tools, data sources and prompts through a common interface. An MCP server exposes capabilities, such as tools that perform actions, resources that provide data, and prompt templates, and an MCP client inside the AI application discovers and calls them using JSON-RPC over transports like stdio or streamable HTTP. Before it, each application needed custom integrations for every tool. With MCP, one server for a system such as a ticketing tool, a database or Kubernetes can be reused by many clients. For platform teams it means a standard way to publish internal capabilities to agents, but also a new security surface: servers must authenticate, authorise per user, validate inputs, rate limit and log, tool descriptions can carry injected instructions, and credentials must be scoped. I treat MCP servers like any production API.
f: What transports does MCP use?
How do you authorise an MCP server per user?
p: MCP standardises how AI apps discover and call tools, resources and prompts exposed by servers, replacing custom integrations. Treat servers as production APIs: authentication, per-user authorisation, validation, rate limits and audit.
cmds: claude mcp add my-server -- node server.js
tip: Say MCP servers need the same security as any API.

q: How do you design tools for an agent so it uses them correctly?
a: Tools are the interface between the model and your systems, so I design them like a good API for a new colleague who cannot ask questions. Each tool has a clear name, a concise description saying when to use it and when not to, and a tight schema with typed, documented parameters and sensible defaults. I prefer a few well-scoped tools to many overlapping ones, because confusion rises with choice. Outputs are concise, structured and informative, returning only what the agent needs, since large dumps waste context, and errors are actionable, saying what went wrong and how to fix the call. I make operations idempotent, add dry-run options, limit blast radius with permissions and quotas, and require confirmation for destructive actions. Then I test with real agent runs, read the transcripts, and refine descriptions where it picks the wrong tool.
f: Why are fewer tools better?
How do you make destructive tools safe?
p: Few, well-scoped tools with clear names and descriptions, typed schemas, concise structured outputs, actionable errors, idempotency, dry-run and confirmation for destructive actions. Refine from transcripts.
tip: Read agent transcripts to find where tool descriptions mislead.

q: How do you limit what an agent can do? Describe least privilege for agents.
a: I assume the model can be tricked or simply make mistakes, so the safety must be in the environment, not in the prompt. Each agent gets its own identity with narrowly scoped, short-lived credentials, only the tools it needs, and read-only access by default. Write actions are restricted by allow lists of resources, environments and commands, and executed through a gateway that enforces policy, rate limits and budgets. High-impact operations, such as deleting data, changing production, spending money or sending external messages, require human approval, with a clear summary of what will happen. Code execution happens in a sandbox with no ambient credentials, limited network and resource caps. Every action is logged with the agent identity, the user on whose behalf it acts, inputs and outcomes, and there is a kill switch. Finally, I test with adversarial inputs to see what a compromised agent could actually do.
f: Why short-lived credentials?
What actions always need human approval?
p: Give each agent its own scoped, short-lived identity, read-only defaults, allow-listed tools and resources, a policy gateway, human approval for high-impact actions, a sandbox for code, full audit logs and a kill switch.
tip: Put safety in the environment, not in the prompt.

q: What is the ReAct pattern and how do planning and reflection improve agents?
a: ReAct, reasoning and acting, interleaves the model's reasoning with tool use: it thinks about what to do, takes an action, observes the result, and reasons again, which grounds its decisions in real feedback instead of guessing. Planning adds an explicit step where the agent breaks a goal into subtasks before executing, which helps with long tasks and lets you review or constrain the plan. Reflection or self-critique has the agent check its own result against the goal, notice mistakes, and retry, which can catch errors but also costs more tokens and can loop. In production I combine these with limits: a maximum number of steps, a token and cost budget, loop detection for repeated identical calls, and checkpoints where progress is saved. For reliability I prefer plans that are visible and verifiable, and external checks like tests or validators over asking the model to simply be careful.
f: How do you detect an agent stuck in a loop?
Why prefer external verification over self-critique?
p: ReAct alternates reasoning and tool actions grounded in observations; planning decomposes tasks; reflection checks results. Bound them with step, token and cost limits, loop detection and external validators.
cmds: pytest -q  # external check after agent edit
tip: Say external tests beat asking the model to be careful.

q: How do you handle memory and state in agents across steps and sessions?
a: I distinguish several kinds of memory. Working memory is the current context window, which holds the task, recent steps and tool results; I keep it small by summarising or dropping verbose outputs. Short-term session state, such as the plan and progress, is stored outside the model in a database or file, so the agent can resume after a failure. Long-term memory stores durable facts and preferences, with retrieval, using a vector or key-value store, and I include only relevant items in each prompt. I make memory writes deliberate, because blindly saving everything creates noise, stale facts and privacy risk. Memory entries carry timestamps and sources, can be reviewed and deleted by users, and are scoped per user or tenant. For long-running tasks, I use checkpoints and idempotent steps, so retries do not repeat side effects, and I treat remembered text as untrusted input because it may contain injected instructions.
f: What should never be stored in memory?
How do checkpoints help with retries?
p: Keep working memory small, store plan and progress externally with checkpoints, use retrieval-based long-term memory with deliberate writes, timestamps and per-user scope, and treat remembered text as untrusted.
cmds: SELECT fact FROM memory WHERE user_id=$1 ORDER BY embedding <=> $2 LIMIT 5;
tip: Mention privacy, deletion and treating memory as untrusted input.

q: What are multi-agent systems, and when are they worth the complexity?
a: A multi-agent system uses several model-driven agents with different roles, tools and prompts that collaborate, for example a planner, a researcher, a coder and a reviewer, either coordinated by an orchestrator or communicating directly. The advantages are specialisation, smaller focused contexts, parallel work, and the possibility of independent review, which can improve quality on complex tasks. The disadvantages are real: more tokens and cost, higher latency, harder debugging because behaviour emerges from interactions, error propagation between agents, and a larger security surface. I try a single agent with good tools first, and move to multiple agents when a task naturally splits into independent parts, needs isolation of permissions, or benefits from a separate verifier. I keep roles and handoffs explicit, log each message, set budgets, and evaluate end to end, because adding agents does not guarantee better results.
f: What is an orchestrator-worker pattern?
How do you debug multi-agent failures?
p: Multiple role-specific agents can specialise, parallelise and cross-check, but cost more and are harder to debug and secure. Start with one agent and split only for independent parts, permission isolation or independent review.
tip: Start single-agent and justify each extra agent.

q: How do you test and evaluate agents, given that their behaviour varies between runs?
a: I evaluate outcomes and behaviour across many runs. I build a suite of tasks with a clear success check, such as a test that passes, a state in a sandbox environment, or a rubric, and run each task several times to measure the success rate and variance, not a single outcome. I track efficiency, steps, tokens, cost and time, plus safety metrics: forbidden actions attempted, tool errors and policy violations. Tool calls are mocked or run in a sandbox so tests are repeatable and safe. I keep transcripts and review failures by hand to find patterns such as wrong tool choice, loops or lost context, then fix prompts, tools or limits and add the case to the suite. Regression runs gate changes to the model, prompt or tools. In production I sample real runs for review, and monitor success proxies like task completion and user corrections.
f: Why run each task several times?
How do you sandbox tools for tests?
p: Build a task suite with automatic success checks, run each task multiple times for success rate and variance, track cost and safety violations, use sandboxed tools, review transcripts of failures and gate changes on regression runs.
tip: Report success rate across runs, not one run.

q: How would you build an on-call assistant agent for SRE, and what safeguards does it need?
a: I would start read-only. The agent receives an alert, gathers context through tools: recent deployments, relevant dashboards and metrics queries, logs, traces, runbooks retrieved from the knowledge base, and the service owner. It correlates these and produces a summary with the likely cause, the evidence and suggested next steps, linking each claim to the source. That alone saves minutes during an incident. Later, I may allow low-risk actions, such as running a diagnostic command, restarting a stateless pod in staging, or opening a ticket, each behind an allow list and approval. Safeguards include least-privilege credentials, no direct production writes without a human confirming, rate limits, an audit trail, protection against injected instructions in logs, a clear display of uncertainty, and a feedback button to measure usefulness. I would run it in shadow mode on past incidents first and measure accuracy before trusting it live.
f: How would you measure usefulness?
Which actions would you never automate?
p: Start read-only: gather alerts, deploys, metrics, logs and runbooks, then summarise cause and evidence with links. Add low-risk actions behind approvals, least privilege, audit and injection defences; validate in shadow mode first.
tip: Say shadow mode on historical incidents comes before live use.

q: What is the difference between synchronous agents and long-running, asynchronous agent workflows, and how do you run them reliably?
a: A synchronous agent answers within a single request, which is fine for tasks that take seconds. Many useful tasks, like researching, migrating code or triaging a backlog, take minutes or hours, so they must be asynchronous. I run them as durable jobs: the request creates a task record and returns an ID, a worker executes the agent loop, state and progress are persisted after each step, and the client polls, subscribes or receives a webhook when it finishes. Workflow engines such as Temporal or a queue with a state store give retries, timeouts, resumption after crashes and visibility. Steps with side effects are idempotent or use idempotency keys. I set overall budgets and deadlines, allow cancellation, request human approval at checkpoints through a pause-and-resume mechanism, and emit traces so progress is observable. This turns an agent from a demo into a dependable service.
f: Why use idempotency keys?
How does pause-and-resume work for approvals?
p: Run long agents as durable jobs with a task ID, persisted state after each step, a workflow engine or queue for retries and resumption, idempotent side effects, budgets, cancellation, approval checkpoints and tracing.
tip: Name durable execution and idempotency keys.

q: How do you observe and debug agent behaviour in production?
a: I trace every run end to end. Each request gets a trace ID, and each model call, tool call, retrieval and decision becomes a span with inputs, outputs, latency, token counts, model version and cost, following OpenTelemetry conventions where possible, with sensitive fields redacted. This lets me replay what happened for any failure. Dashboards show success rate, steps per task, tool error rates, cost per task, latency percentiles, loop and limit hits, and guardrail triggers, and alerts fire on anomalies such as a spike in cost or a tool failing. Because outputs are non-deterministic, I keep transcripts for sampled and failed runs, support user feedback signals, and can replay a run against a new prompt or model offline. This is the same observability discipline as for services, extended with token and quality signals.
